newsitem.title: CANADA: Reuters poll shows huge Liberal lead in Canada.
newsitem.headline: Reuters poll shows huge Liberal lead in Canada.

text.p: Prime Minister Jean Chretien has maintained a crushing lead over his rivals going into the June 2 federal election despite a rocky first week of his re-election campaign, a Reuters poll showed on Monday.

In the first poll taken since Chretien called the election on April 27, his Liberal Party nonetheless appeared to have suffered in the prairies, where many voters have expressed anger that elections were called despite severe flooding.
But over the entire country, the survey conducted by the Zogby International polling firm put the Liberals at 47.6 percent of decided voters, more than 30 points ahead of their nearest rivals.

"Chretien has remarkable strength. He even has the support of those who have been victimised by the economy," said John Zogby, who was the pollster closest to forecasting the eventual margin of victory in last year's U.S. presidential election.
The poll of 1,005 likely Canadian voters, conducted from May 1-4, meant Chretien would return with another majority government if the numbers held until June 2.
However, Canadian voters have shown increasing volatility in recent years, and the Reuters-Zogby poll showed one in four undecided with four weeks to go.
Chretien, 63, called the election 1-1/2 years before he had to to capitalise on his strong polling numbers, but found it hard to list any issue that necessitated an early election.

He was attacked on the right by the Reform Party and the Conservative Party for releasing an electoral platform that offered billions of dollars of new spending rather than early tax cuts. On the left, he came under fire from the New Democratic Party (NDP) for cutting social programmes.

Yet the poll put the Conservatives -- who were swept from power in 1993 -- far behind the Liberals at 16.2 percent, with Reform at 15.4 percent, the NDP at 10.2 percent and the separatist Bloc Quebecois at 7.7 percent.
In Ontario, the most populous province, the Liberal lead looked insurmountable at 60.2 percent to the Conservatives' 18.1 percent, with 10.1 percent for Reform and the NDP.

In Quebec, the second most populous, the poll gave the Liberals a 42.9 to 31.3 percent lead over the Bloc Quebecois and found 59.1 percent of Quebeckers would vote against sovereignty compared with 40.9 percent in favour.

Reform trailed the Liberals narrowly in British Columbia and led in its home base of Alberta. But it showed unprecedented strength in the prairie provinces of Manitoba and Saskatchewan, leading the Liberals at 35.5 to 25.4 percent, with the NDP at 20.6 percent.

"There is decidedly more anger from Manitoba west," Zogby said. Of western voters, 68 percent to 17 percent said there was no good reason to call the election now, and the numbers were even worse, 79 to 8 percent, in the flood-hit prairies.
And 33.1 percent of voters said they were financially worse off than four years ago, compared with 19 percent who said they were better off.
When voters were asked, parties aside, to say who was best suited to be prime minister, youthful Conservative Jean Charest led Chretien by a two-to-one margin.
But both Chretien and Charest received strong favourable ratings, by 65.1 percent and 56.6 percent respectively of those polled. And most voters felt Canada was heading in the right direction.
A majority (55.7 percent) said the government should focus more on reducing the government deficit than on increased spending (29.0 percent).
Two in three (66.8 percent) wanted a broad-based tax cut, though 49.4 percent said this should wait until after the deficit was eliminated.
Zogby said the poll would carry a national margin of error of 3.2 percentage points 19 times out of 20, while in smaller regional samples the margin of error would be greater.
